# Education in Sweden
Education in Sweden is structured as a progression from preschool (Förskola, ages 1–6) and preschool class (Förskoleklass, 6–7), into compulsory education (Grundskola) lasting nine years for ages 7–16, divided into lower, middle, and upper stages. Compulsory schooling is mandatory for children between the ages of six–seven and fifteen–sixteen. Students study 16 core subjects, starting foreign language instruction in grade 6, and receive letter grades (A–F) from year 6 onward. National tests are administered in grades 3, 6, and 9. After compulsory school, students may enter elective upper secondary education (Gymnasieskola) for three years, choosing from 18 preparatory or vocational national programmes. Eligibility for upper secondary is based on passing specific subjects at the compulsory level, with additional introductory programmes available for those not meeting requirements.
Higher education in Sweden includes universities and university colleges, offering degrees at three cycles: bachelor's (first cycle, 3 years), master's (second cycle, 1–2 years), and doctoral (third cycle, up to 4 years). Admission requires completion of upper secondary school and demonstration of proficiency in Swedish and English, with additional standardized testing (SweSAT) used for university entry. Grading varies between institutions but can be converted to the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS). Independent schools ("friskolor") are publicly funded, cannot charge fees, and serve both primary and secondary levels, while higher vocational education offers specialized post-secondary paths outside the traditional university system. Sweden has initiated reforms in response to criticisms on educational standards and equity, with ongoing debates regarding the role and regulation of for-profit and religious independent schools.
